questions.stem: What does « à mon avis » mean?
questions.explanation: « À mon avis » opens an opinion and is the phrase to reach for in any discussion task. « Un avis » is an opinion; « un conseil » is advice, which is the false friend lurking in the third option.

questions.stem: What does « je pense que » mean?
questions.explanation: « Penser » is to think. « Je pense que » must be followed by a full clause, so « je pense que c'est bien » — not just « je pense bien », which means something else entirely.
« Parce que » gives a reason and is the connective that turns an opinion into an argument. « Bien que » is 'although' and takes the subjunctive, which is why it is taught separately.
« Cependant » signals a contrast, like « pourtant » and « néanmoins ». « Donc » is 'therefore' and points the other way, so mixing them up reverses the logic of a sentence.
« Le travail » is work. English 'travel' is « le voyage » — a false friend that catches almost everyone, and the reason the second option is here.
« Actuellement » means currently or at present. English 'actually' is « en fait ». This pair is one of the most common false friends in written work, and it changes the meaning of a whole sentence.
« Éventuellement » means possibly, not eventually — English 'eventually' is « finalement » or « à la fin ». It is the mirror image of the « actuellement » trap.

questions.stem: What does « sensible » mean in French?
questions.explanation: « Sensible » means sensitive. English 'sensible' is « raisonnable ». Because the word exists in both languages with different meanings, it slips past a reader who is not looking for it.
« Une librairie » sells books; a library is « une bibliothèque ». The two are the standard example of a false friend in every French course, and worth learning as a pair.

questions.stem: Which phrase best introduces a counter-argument?
questions.explanation: « D'un autre côté » is 'on the other hand'. The others also structure an argument but do different jobs: giving an example, summing up, and opening a first point.

questions.stem: What does « je suis d'accord » mean?
questions.explanation: « Être d'accord » is to agree, and it uses « être » rather than « avoir ». To disagree is « je ne suis pas d'accord » — the standard negative wrapped around the verb.

questions.explanation: « Il faut » is impersonal and has no real subject — the « il » stands for nothing. It is followed by an infinitive: « il faut partir », meaning one must leave.

questions.stem: What does « avoir besoin de » mean?
questions.explanation: Literally 'to have need of'. French builds several states this way with « avoir » where English uses 'to be' or a modal — « avoir envie de » for 'to feel like' works the same way.
« Quand même » is an idiom and cannot be worked out from « quand » and « même » separately. It is extremely common in speech and signals mild concession or surprise.

questions.stem: What does « faire les courses » mean?
questions.explanation: « Faire les courses » is grocery shopping; « faire du shopping » is browsing for clothes. « Une course » on its own can be a race, which is where the running option comes from.
« Se débrouiller » means to get by or sort yourself out, and it is one of the most useful verbs in real conversation. It is reflexive, so it always carries a pronoun.

« Un stage » is a work placement, and « un stagiaire » is an intern. The theatre stage is « la scène ». It appears constantly in Year 10 work-and-future-plans topics, which is where the false friend does most damage.

questions.stem: Which phrase means 'in my view, it is essential that'?
options: À moi, il est essentiel que
Selon moi, il est essentiel que
questions.explanation: « Selon moi » is a standard alternative to « à mon avis ». The last option translates 'in my opinion' word for word and produces « dans mon avis », which is not French.

questions.stem: Which sentence best expresses 'I would rather stay at home'?
options: Je préférerais de rester à la maison
Je préférerais rester à la maison
questions.explanation: « Préférer » in the conditional gives the polite 'would rather', and it is followed directly by an infinitive with no preposition. Adding « de » is the commonest error, and « à la maison » is the fixed phrase for 'at home'.

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'the more I study, the more I understand'?
options: Le plus j'étudie, plus je comprends
Plus que j'étudie, plus je comprends
Plus j'étudie, le plus je comprends
questions.explanation: French uses a bare « plus … plus … » with no article and no « que ». English 'the more … the more' tempts you to insert articles, and every wrong option here does exactly that.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have been waiting for an hour'?
options: Je suis en attente une heure
questions.explanation: Two traps at once: « attendre » means to wait *for* and takes no preposition, and « depuis » with an ongoing action keeps the present tense. English pushes you towards both errors simultaneously.

questions.stem: Which best translates 'I miss my family'?
questions.explanation: « Manquer » reverses the roles: the thing missed becomes the subject, so it is literally 'my family is missing to me'. Translating directly gives the second option, which means you failed to attend them.
